rules.title: Coverage and exemptions determining whether Berkeley rent increase limits apply
rules.requirement: Berkeley’s rent increase limits apply only to fully covered units; partially covered units are registered and subject to just-cause eviction and security-deposit-interest rules, but not rent control. The documents identify which unit types are fully covered, partially covered, or exempt, including Measure BB changes for some subsidized units and shared kitchen/bath units.
rules.coverage_conditions: Most units in multifamily properties built before 1980 are fully covered.; Single-family homes with current tenancies that began before 1996 are fully covered.; Single-family homes are fully covered if the current tenancy began before 1996.; Single-family homes with five or more rooms rented out individually with separate leases are fully covered.; Rooming-house coverage applies where five or more rooms are rented individually with separate leases.; Some government-subsidized units are fully or partially covered depending on unit type.
rules.exemptions: New construction units with a certificate of occupancy issued after June 1980 are partially covered, not rent-controlled.; Single-family homes with a tenancy that began on or after January 1, 1996 are partially covered, not rent-controlled.; Single-family homes with tenancies beginning on or after January 1, 1996 are partially covered, not rent-controlled.; Most condominiums are partially covered, not rent-controlled.; Units with Section 202 or Section 811 subsidies are partially covered regardless of unit type because rent control is prohibited by other law.; These subsidized units are partially covered regardless of unit type if the project has a HUD-insured or HUD-held mortgage.; Golden duplexes are exempt.; Golden duplex exemption requires owner occupancy.; A unit where the owner shares a kitchen or bath with the tenant is exempt if the owner lived on the property at the time the tenancy started.; Shared kitchen/bath units are exempt only if the owner lived on the property at the start of the tenancy.; Tenancies started after Nov 7, 2018, on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied are exempt.; ADU exemption applies to tenancies started after Nov 7, 2018.; ADU exemption requires owner occupancy in either unit.; University rental units such as dormitories are exempt.; Nonprofit cooperatives are exempt.

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance as amended by Measure BB
rules.requirement: Berkeley’s Rent Ordinance requires just cause for eviction in fully and partially covered units, and the documents describe several Measure BB changes: nonpayment eviction is barred unless rental debt is at least one month of HUD Fair Market Rent for an equivalent-size unit; tenants cannot be evicted for refusing to sign a substantially similar lease; lease-breach evictions require a mutually agreed material term, substantial actual harm, unreasonable tenant behavior, and detailed notice; and termination notices and related filings must include specified Rent Board information and be filed with the Rent Board within three business days.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to tenants in units fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance.
rules.exemptions: Tenancies started after Nov. 7, 2018 on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied are exempt.; University rental units such as dormitories are exempt.; Nonprofit cooperatives are exempt.; Owner shares a kitchen or bath with the tenant and lived on the property at the time the tenancy started.; Golden duplexes are exempt.
rules.interaction: supersedes CA-JC-01 where it covers the unit
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: In Berkeley, tenants in units that are fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance cannot be evicted unless there is "just cause” (previously called “good cause”). Measure BB has changed some just causes, eliminated one just cause, added new requirements for eviction notices, and shortened the timeline for landlords to file copies of certain eviction-related documents with the Rent Board.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2024-02-06 (utility-rule effective date mentioned in same Measure BB summary, D006)

rules.title: Tenant screening fee disclosure and nonrefundable existing-tenancy application fee ban
rules.requirement: Berkeley Municipal Code chapter 13.78 requires owners who charge an application/screening fee to provide a tenant screening fee rights statement and the maximum state-law fee cap before taking the fee. It also prohibits non-refundable fees charged to existing tenants for renewing a tenancy or for roommate-change requests in a pre-existing household, and makes contrary lease terms unenforceable.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to owners or agents of residential rental property in Berkeley who charge an application/screening fee.; The non-refundable fee prohibition applies to fees charged to existing tenants for renewal or roommate-change requests in a pre-existing household.
rules.interaction:
There are limits on the amount of and uses for tenant screening and application fees under state and local law.

Applicability to Existing Rental Agreements (BMC 13.78.018)
Chapter 13.78 applies to all residential rental agreements regardless of any contractual language in any rental agreement or lease to the contrary. Any provision of an existing rental agreement or lease that violates the provisions of this chapter are unenforceable.
rules.quoted_span: When an owner or the owner’s agent gets a request to rent residential property in Berkeley from an applicant and the owner charges a fee to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application, the owner must provide, either in the rental application or in a separate disclosure before receiving the fee, a clear and conspicuous tenant screening fee rights statement and a statement of the maximum fee cap permitted under
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents

rules.title: Ronald V. Dellums Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance
rules.requirement: Berkeley prohibits rental housing providers from asking about or using criminal history or criminal background checks in rental advertising, applications, tenant selection, or decision-making, with listed exceptions. The ordinance also requires written notice and an opportunity to respond before adverse action based on criminal history.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental housing providers in Berkeley and current or prospective tenants.
rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders.; Public housing/Section 8 properties have limited exemptions.; Owner-occupied properties between 1 and 3 units where an owner of record resides in one unit as a primary residence.; Units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back to their home in accordance with BMC 13.76.130 A.9.; Units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates.
rules.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents
rules.penalty: Administrative fines of at least $1,000 and up to $10,000 per violation, civil damages including actual damages or three times the amount of one month's rent, punitive damages, attorneys' fees and costs, and injunctive relief.

rules.title: Berkeley prohibition on coordinated pricing algorithms for residential rents or occupancy
rules.requirement: Berkeley Municipal Code chapter 13.63 prohibits selling, licensing, or otherwise providing coordinated pricing algorithms to Berkeley landlords for residential units, and prohibits landlords from using those algorithms to set rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in Berkeley. Each separate month a violation continues, and each separate residential dwelling unit for which a landlord used the algorithm, is a separate violation.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.
rules.exemptions: Excluded are aggregated and anonymous reports, studies, or presentations that do not recommend future rent prices, fees, occupancy rates, or other rental contract terms.; Excluded are products used to establish rent or income limits under affordable housing guidelines of a government or political subdivision.; Excluded are products or processes used for project-financing market research, appraisals, or research, testing, or training for software development, including model development/training/testing so long as competitor data is not used as an input when a recommendation is calculated for publication or provision to a Berkeley landlord.
rules.interaction:
F. This Chapter is not intended to prevent the development or sale of software to help 
landlords manage their units generally or through the use of public data. Nor does this 
Chapter regulate the amount of rent that a landlord may charge. This Chapter solely 
regulates the use and sale of the coordinated pricing algorithms, to prevent the harms 
described above.
rules.quoted_span:
A. It shall be unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to City of Berkeley 
landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy 
levels that may be achieved for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley. 
B. It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use a coordinated pricing algorithm described 
in subsection A when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in 
the City of Berkeley. Each separate month that a violation exists or continues, and each 
separate residential dwelling unit for which the landlord used the coordinated pricing 
algorithm, shall constitute a separate and distinct violation.
rules.penalty: The City Attorney may seek damages, injunctive relief, restitution/return of illegal profits, and/or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation; aggrieved tenants may seek injunctive relief, money damages, and/or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation; prevailing City Attorney or tenant receives reasonable attorney’s fees and costs.

rules.title: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
rules.requirement: Housing providers receiving specified City-supported funding, land, or inclusionary units may not use blanket criminal-record exclusions and must assess applicants case by case; they also may not consider certain arrests, non-convictions, juvenile records, or convictions older than 5 years. The policy also bars use of applicant credit score to approve or deny housing applications, while allowing limited use of credit history only in lieu of rental history when rental history is unavailable.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to housing providers receiving DND funding and/or land.; Also applies to housing providers with income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy.
rules.interaction:
Where federal or state law imposes a criminal history requirement that conflicts with a 
requirement of this guidance, the federal or state law preempts this policy.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
rules.quoted_span:
Housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development (DND) funding and/or 
land, or that have income restricted units created under the Boston Planning and Development 
Agency (BPDA) Inclusionary Development Policy will not impose a blanket policy that denies 
housing to anyone with arrests and or convictions. Housing providers will consider applicants on 
a case-by-case basis.

rules.title: Statewide rent cap under the Tenant Protection Act
rules.requirement: California caps rent increases for covered residential units at the lower of 5% plus the applicable cost-of-living change or 10% over any 12-month period, measured from the lowest gross rental rate charged during the prior 12 months. The law also limits increases for the same tenant to no more than two increments in a 12-month period, exempts specified properties, and yields to stricter local rent or price controls.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to owners of residential real property increasing the gross rental rate for a dwelling or unit over a 12-month period.; Applies only after the initial rental rate for a new tenancy has been established.
rules.exemptions: Affordable or subsidized housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction, recorded document, or subsidy agreement is exempt.; Dormitories owned and operated by specified schools are exempt.; Housing subject to stricter public-entity rent or price control is exempt from this state cap.; Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years is exempt, unless it is a mobilehome.; Separately alienable residential real property, including a mobilehome, is exempt if ownership and notice conditions are met.; For the separately alienable-property exemption, the owner cannot be a REIT.; For the separately alienable-property exemption, the owner cannot be a corporation.; For the separately alienable-property exemption, the owner cannot be an LLC with at least one corporate member.; For the separately alienable-property exemption, the owner cannot be management of a mobilehome park.; For the separately alienable-property exemption, tenants must receive the statutory written exemption notice.; A two-unit single structure with owner occupancy at the beginning of the tenancy is exempt if the owner continues in occupancy and neither unit is an ADU or JADU.
rules.interaction: yields to SA-RENT-01 where that rule covers the unit
rules.quoted_span: (a) (1)   Subject to subdivision (b), an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2019-03-15 (applies to covered non-mobilehome rent increases occurring on or after this date, D024); 2021-02-18 (applies to covered mobilehome rent increases occurring on or after this date, D024)
rules.penalty: An owner who demands, accepts, receives, or retains rent above the maximum allowed is liable for injunctive relief, excess-rent damages, attorney’s fees and costs, and potentially treble damages; the Attorney General and local government attorneys may enforce and seek injunctive relief.

rules.title: California statewide just-cause eviction protections
rules.requirement: After a tenant has lawfully occupied covered residential property for the statutory period, the owner may terminate the tenancy only for stated at-fault or no-fault just cause. For no-fault terminations, the owner must provide relocation assistance or a final-month rent waiver equal to one month of rent, and numerous property types are exempt.
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenant must have continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 12 months, or in some multi-adult tenancies all tenants for 12 months or one tenant for 24 months.
rules.exemptions: Transient and tourist hotel occupancy.; Housing accommodations in nonprofit hospitals, religious facilities, extended care facilities, licensed residential care facilities for the elderly, or adult residential facilities.; Dormitories owned and operated by certain schools.; Tenant shares bathroom or kitchen facilities with owner who maintains principal residence at the property.; Single-family owner-occupied residences where owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms, including an ADU or JADU.; A mobilehome under the single-family owner-occupied residences exemption.; Property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure where owner occupied one unit as principal residence at beginning of tenancy, continues in occupancy, and neither unit is an ADU or JADU.; Property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure where owner occupied one unit as principal residence at beginning of tenancy and continues in occupancy.; Neither unit is an accessory dwelling unit or a junior accessory dwelling unit.; Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless the housing is a mobilehome.; Residential real property, including a mobilehome, alienable separate from title to any other dwelling unit, if owner-type and notice conditions are met.; Owner is not a real estate investment trust.; Owner is not a corporation.; Owner is not a limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation.; Owner is not management of a mobilehome park.; Tenants were provided the statutory written exemption notice.; Housing restricted or subsidized as affordable housing for very low, low, or moderate income persons and families.; Residential real property subject to a qualifying local just-cause ordinance instead of this section.; Homeowner of a mobilehome, as defined in Section 798.9.
rules.interaction: yields to SA-JC-01 where that rule covers the unit
rules.quoted_span: (a) Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2026-01-01 (amendment, D023)
rules.penalty: Owner’s failure to comply can void the notice, and material violations can support actual damages, attorney’s fees and costs, punitive or treble damages, and injunctive relief.

rules.title: California residential security deposit cap
rules.requirement: For residential tenancies, a landlord generally may not demand or receive security above one month’s rent, plus first month’s rent. A small-landlord exception allows up to two months’ rent if the landlord is a natural person or qualifying LLC and owns no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four total dwelling units; that exception does not apply to prospective tenants who are service members.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property used as the tenant's dwelling.; Small-landlord higher cap applies only if the landlord is a natural person or an LLC whose members are all natural persons.; Small-landlord higher cap applies only if the landlord owns no more than two residential rental properties.; Small-landlord higher cap applies only if those properties collectively include no more than four dwelling units offered for rent.
rules.exemptions: The cap does not prohibit an advance payment of at least six months' rent for a lease term of six months or longer.; The cap does not preclude a mutual agreement for specified tenant-requested structural, decorative, furnishing, or similar alterations.; The amended subdivision does not apply to security collected or demanded before July 1, 2024.; The two-month small-landlord exception does not apply if the prospective tenant is a service member.
rules.quoted_span: Except as provided in paragraph (2), (3), or (5), a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2025-04-01 (operative date for service-member written statement and return of additional amount of security, D025); 2024-07-01 (exception does not apply to security collected or demanded before this date, D025)
rules.penalty: Bad faith claim or retention of the security in violation of this section may subject the landlord to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages.

rules.title: California application screening fee limits and procedures
rules.requirement: California allows landlords or their agents to charge an application screening fee only to cover actual screening costs, subject to a statutory cap adjusted annually by CPI. The law also requires availability and processing safeguards, receipts, refunds of unused amounts, and delivery of the consumer credit report.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies when a landlord or agent receives a request to rent residential property from an applicant.
rules.interaction:
(k) The application screening fee shall not be considered an “advance fee” as that term is used in Section 10026 of the Business and Professions Code, and shall not be considered “security” as that term is used in Section 1950.5.
(l) This section is not intended to preempt any provisions or regulations that govern the collection of deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs.
rules.quoted_span:
(b) The amount of the application screening fee shall not be greater than the actual
out-of-pocket costs of gathering information concerning the applicant, including, but not limited to, the cost of using a tenant screening service or a consumer credit reporting service, and the reasonable value of time spent by the landlord or their agent in obtaining information on the applicant. In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant. The thirty dollar ($30) application screening fee may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998.

rules.title: Fair housing law bars source-of-income discrimination and sets screening rules for subsidized applicants
rules.requirement: California fair housing law prohibits denying or making housing unavailable because of source of income, including Section 8 and other subsidies. Where there is a government rent subsidy, landlords may not use an income standard based on the full rent and may not use credit history without offering the applicant the option to provide lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of ability to pay the tenant portion.
rules.key_value: No SOI bias; subsidy screening limits
rules.quoted_span:
(o) (1) In instances in which there is a government rent subsidy, to do either of the following:
(A) Use a financial or income standard in assessing eligibility for the rental of housing that is not based on the portion of the rent to be paid by the tenant.
(B) (i) Use a person’s credit history as part of the application process for a rental accommodation without offering the applicant the option, at the applicant’s discretion, of providing lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of the applicant’s reasonable ability to pay
the portion of the rent to be paid by the tenant, including, but not limited to, government benefit payments, pay records, and bank statements.

rules.title: Application screening fee limits and timing rules
rules.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and no more than $30 per applicant, adjusted annually by CPI. A landlord may not charge the fee when no unit is or will be available within a reasonable time, and may charge it only under specified processing/refund procedures, including not charging unless the application is actually considered or refunding unselected applicants under an alternative process.
rules.interaction:
(l) This section is not intended
to preempt any provisions or regulations that govern the collection of deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs.
rules.quoted_span:
(b) The amount of the application screening fee shall not be greater than the actual
out-of-pocket costs of gathering information concerning the applicant, including, but not limited to, the cost of using a tenant screening service or a consumer credit reporting service, and the reasonable value of time spent by the landlord or their agent in obtaining information on the applicant. In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant. The thirty dollar ($30) application screening fee may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998.
(c) (1) A landlord or their agent shall not charge an applicant an application screening fee when they know or should have known that no rental unit is available at that time or will be available within a reasonable period of time.

rules.title: Fair housing law restricts criminal-history screening
rules.requirement: California fair housing law, as described by the Civil Rights Department, says housing providers cannot consider certain criminal-history records and cannot impose blanket bans on all applicants with criminal history. If denying based on a conviction, the conviction must be directly related to the applicant's ability to be a good tenant and not threaten health, safety, or property, considering the nature and severity of the crime and the time since the conduct.
rules.citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (housing discrimination provisions)
rules.quoted_span:
Can a housing provider consider an applicant’s criminal history in deciding whether or not to rent to them?
Yes.  Generally, a housing provider may check the criminal history of an applicant, but there are some limitations. Housing  providers cannot consider some types of criminal history including arrests that did not lead to a conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or records or matters processed in the juvenile justice system. Housing providers are also prohibited from having “blanket bans” of all people with a criminal history.
If a housing provider intends to deny someone’s application based on a criminal conviction, it must be directly-related to someone’s ability to be a good tenant and to not be a threat to the health and safety of others and the property. In determining whether a criminal conviction is directly-related, a housing provider should consider the nature and severity of the crime and the amount of time that has passed since the criminal conduct occurred.
citation_aliases: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (housing discrimination provisions)
rules.raw_citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (housing discrimination provisions)
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents

rules.title: Common pricing algorithms are unlawful when used as part of a Cartwright Act restraint of trade or when used coercively
rules.requirement: California prohibits using or distributing a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination, or conspiracy that restrains trade or commerce, and separately prohibits using or distributing such an algorithm to coerce another person to adopt the algorithm’s recommended price or commercial term for the same or similar products or services in California. The law defines a common pricing algorithm broadly to include technology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term.
rules.interaction: (c) Nothing in this section shall impair or limit the applicability of antitrust laws.
rules.quoted_span:
(a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
(b) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm if the person coerces another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by the common pricing algorithm for the same or similar products or services in the jurisdiction of this state.
rules.effective_date_note: Cal. Const. art. IV, § 8(c)(1) (regular-session statutes take effect January 1 of the year following enactment)
rules.penalty: AB 325 states that it expands conduct prohibited by the Cartwright Act, 'the violation of which is punishable as a crime.'

rules.title: Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance prohibits housing discrimination based on source of income
rules.requirement: In Cambridge housing transactions, landlords, sellers, and rental agents may not discriminate based on source of income, which includes Section 8 and public benefits. The ordinance covers rental decisions and tenancy terms, while allowing reasonable selection standards if applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.
rules.key_value: Source of income is a protected category in housing discrimination law
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two-family dwellings are exempt.; Owner lives in the two-family dwelling.
rules.quoted_span:
The protected categories under the Cambridge Human Rights Ordinance and the Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance are the following:
Disability – Defined consistent with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) – a physical or mental impairment which substantially limits one or more major life activities
Race
Color
National Origin or Ancestry
Family Status
Source of Income, includes Section 8 and public benefits

rules.penalty: The Commission has the authority to provide various remedies after hearing, including filing a criminal complaint in District Court, levying civil fines of up to $300 for each violation, filing a civil complaint in Superior Court seeking injunctive relief, and seeking an award of damages, expenses and other relief.

rules.title: Hoboken rent control ordinance limits ordinary rent increases in covered units
rules.requirement: For dwelling units covered by Hoboken's rent control chapter, a landlord generally may not charge more than the lesser of 5% or the applicable CPI-based percentage at lease expiration or termination, and may not impose more than one such cost-of-living increase in any 12-month period. The chapter applies to all dwelling units unless a listed exemption applies, including certain newly constructed dwellings, buildings vacant since January 1, 1984, and certain post-1987 multiple dwellings exempt under state-authorized local exemption language incorporated into the code.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to dwelling units as defined in the chapter.; Ordinary capped increases apply at lease expiration or termination, including periodic tenants and leases under one year.
rules.exemptions: Motels and hotels are exempt.; Newly constructed dwellings are exempt for the initial rent or lease agreement if registered before first rental; later rents are covered.; Industrial property is exempt.; Nonresidential and commercial property is exempt, though apartment units in mixed-use buildings remain covered.; Student housing owned or controlled by an educational institution is exempt.; Housing owned and operated by other government agencies is exempt.; A building completely vacant on or before and since January 1, 1984 may qualify for an initial-rent exemption if not made vacant through unlawful means and registered before renting; later rents are covered.; Certain multiple dwellings constructed after June 25, 1987 are exempt for the amortization period of the initial mortgage or 30 years after completion, whichever is less, if statutory notice requirements are met.; Where a governmental agency contract supersedes Hoboken's authority to regulate rents, the chapter is preempted during that contract period.
rules.interaction: supersedes NJ-RENT-01 where it covers the unit
rules.quoted_span: At the expiration of a lease or at the termination of a lease of a periodic tenant, no landlord may request or receive a percentage increase in rent which is greater than 5% or the percentage difference between the consumer price index three months prior to the expiration or termination of the lease and three months prior to the commencement of the lease term, whichever is less. For a periodic tenant or for a tenant whose lease terms shall be less than one year, said tenant shall not suffer or be caused to pay more than one rent increase in any twelve-month period which exceeds 5% or the consumer price index percentage differential for the twelve-month period commencing 15 months prior to and ending three months prior to the effective date of the proposed increase, whichever is less.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2023-02-01 (amendment, S009); 2025-07-09 (amendment, S010)
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents

rules.title: Algorithmic rent fixing in rental housing market prohibited
rules.requirement: Hoboken prohibits landlords from using software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to coordinate, recommend, or implement residential rents, lease terms, or occupancy levels using nonpublic competitor information. Violations may be enforced by the Division of Housing or an aggrieved private citizen in Municipal Court and may be punished by fines up to $2,000 or community service up to 90 days.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords who rent residential dwelling units used as primary residences in Hoboken.
rules.exemptions: Excludes medical, long-term care, and detention facilities from the definition of residential dwelling unit.
rules.quoted_span: Landlords who rent any residential dwelling unit (defined as any primary residence excluding medical/long-term care or detention facilities) in the City of Hoboken are prohibited from price fixing using algorithmic pricing. For purposes of this chapter, "price fixing using algorithmic pricing" shall be defined as the use of software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information from other real estate lessors in order to coordinate, recommend, or implement rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units among competing real estate lessors.
rules.conflict_note: The Hoboken ordinance takes effect earlier and regulates the same subject. The state FAIR Act does not categorically preempt all local ordinances, but starting 2027-07-01 it prohibits municipalities from having ordinances that conflict with the act. Because both laws regulate algorithmic rent-setting and the record does not expressly state whether Hoboken's ordinance is fully consistent with the state act, the interaction is best classified as possible_conflict from the state act's effective date.
rules.penalty: Upon conviction, penalties may include those prescribed under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5, a fine not exceeding $2,000, or community service not exceeding 90 days.

rules.title: Jersey City Rent Control Ordinance
rules.requirement: Jersey City's Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations administers and enforces the Rent Control Ordinance, Chapter 260 of the Jersey City Municipal Code. The official city page also states that all 1-4 unit properties are exempt from rent control and that the ordinance provides certain exemptions from rent regulation.
rules.exemptions: 1-4 unit properties are exempt from rent control.
rules.interaction: supersedes NJ-RENT-01 where it covers the unit
rules.quoted_span:

Rent Control Ordinance, Chapter 260

rules.title: Jersey City ban on algorithmic rent coordination services
rules.requirement: Jersey City adopted an ordinance prohibiting landlords from using algorithmic rent coordination services to coordinate or recommend rents, lease terms, or occupancy in multifamily housing. Secondary sources indicate the ordinance carries fines up to $2,000 per day and includes public and private enforcement.
rules.quoted_span:
Jersey City, NJ
Jersey City Code § 218-12 (effective June 2025)
Prohibits a landlord’s use of algorithmic rent coordination services; includes public and private enforcement; fines up to $2,000 per day.
rules.conflict_note: The city ordinance takes effect earlier (June 2025) and the state FAIR Act takes effect 2027-07-01. The state text does not categorically preempt all local ordinances, only those that 'conflict with this act.' Because both laws prohibit algorithmic rent coordination and the provided records do not identify any incompatible requirement, the relationship is best characterized as possible_conflict starting on the state effective date, based on the express anti-conflict/preemption language. If no actual conflict exists in application, both may operate cumulatively.
rules.penalty: fines up to $2,000 per day

rules.title: Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance annual allowable rent increase for RSO units
rules.requirement: For rental units subject to Los Angeles's Rent Stabilization Ordinance, rent may be increased once every 12 months by the City's allowable annual percentage. The documents state the allowable increase was 3% from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026, and that beginning February 2, 2026 landlords may no longer add any extra percentage for utilities.

rules.title: Los Angeles Just Cause for Eviction Ordinance (JCO)
rules.requirement: The JCO prohibits termination of covered tenancies without just cause and allows only specified at-fault and no-fault reasons for eviction; no-fault evictions require relocation assistance and filing with LAHD. It generally covers residential properties in Los Angeles not regulated by the RSO, once the tenant has occupied the unit for at least six months or the original lease has expired, whichever comes first.
rules.coverage_conditions: Covers most residential properties in Los Angeles not regulated by the RSO.; Applies to a tenancy once the tenant has lived in the unit at least six months or the original lease has expired, whichever comes first.; Can apply to buildings newer than October 1, 1978.; Can apply to a property containing only one single-family dwelling.
rules.exemptions: Transient hotels are excepted from the JCO.; Licensed care facilities are excepted from the JCO.; Fraternity or sorority houses are excepted from the JCO.; Owner’s roommate situations are excepted from the JCO.; Some cooperatives are excepted from the JCO.; Some nonprofit homeless facilities or short-term substance-abuse treatment centers are excepted.; Some HACLA-owned or government-owned properties are excepted.

rules.title: Massachusetts generally prohibits local rent control, with a narrow opt-in exception framework
rules.requirement: Massachusetts law bars cities and towns from enacting, maintaining, or enforcing rent control unless a municipality accepts Chapter 40P, and even then any rent control regulation must be voluntary after six months, cannot cover certain subjects or smaller landlords/units above a rent threshold, and must compensate owners from municipal general funds.
rules.exemptions: Municipalities that accept Chapter 40P may adopt rent control only if the regulation becomes entirely voluntary after six months for property owners.; Any local rent control regulation may not apply to units owned by a person or entity owning fewer than 10 rental units.; Any local rent control regulation may not apply to units with fair market rent above $400.

rules.requirement: A 2026 statewide ballot proposal to restore rent control in Massachusetts was struck by the Supreme Judicial Court and cannot go forward. rules.title: Massachusetts security deposit cap and permitted upfront charges
rules.requirement: For residential tenancies, a landlord may require at move-in no more than first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit equal to one month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock. Effective August 1, 2025, regulations may also authorize an optional fee in lieu of a security deposit, but the total fee payments may not exceed one month's rent.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to leases relating to residential real property and to any tenancy at or prior to commencement.; Applies to amounts required at or prior to the commencement of any tenancy.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of 100 days or less for a vacation or recreational purpose.
rules.quoted_span:
(b) At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, no lessor or agent of the lessor may require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay, to the lessor or to an agent of the lessor, any amount in excess of the following:
(i) rent for the first full month of occupancy;  and,
(ii) rent for the last full month of occupancy calculated at the same rate as the first month;  and,
(iii) a security deposit equal to the first month's rent provided that such security deposit is deposited as required by subsection (3) and that the tenant is given the statement of condition as required by subsection (2);  provided, however, that the executive office of housing and livable communities may promulgate regulations to authorize a lessor and a tenant or prospective tenant to agree to the payment of a fee in lieu of payment of a security deposit;
rules.penalty: If the lessor fails to comply with clauses (a), (d), or (e) of subsection 6, the tenant shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of such security deposit or balance thereof to which the tenant is entitled plus interest at the rate of five per cent from the date when such payment became due, together with court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

rules.title: Massachusetts broker/finder fee rule for rental housing
rules.requirement: Only a licensed broker or salesperson may charge a fee for finding dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants. Any fee may be paid only by the party—landlord or tenant—who originally engaged and contracted with the licensed broker or salesperson.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to charging a fee for finding dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants.; Applies to contracts to find rental residential real property for a tenant or to find a tenant for a property.
rules.quoted_span: A licensed broker or salesperson may solely contract with a prospective tenant to find rental residential real property for a tenant and present an offer to lease to the landlord or landlord's agent and negotiate on behalf of the tenant or may solely contract with a landlord or landlord's agent to find a tenant for a property.  Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.

rules.title: Massachusetts limits upfront rental charges and authorizes optional fee-in-lieu of security deposit by regulation
rules.requirement: At or before the start of a residential tenancy, a landlord or landlord's agent may require only first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit up to one month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock. The statute also authorizes regulations allowing an optional fee in lieu of a security deposit, with the total fee capped at no more than one month's rent.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential tenancies.; Applies to amounts required at or before tenancy commencement.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to vacation or recreational occupancies of 100 days or less.
rules.quoted_span:

rules.title: Public assistance and housing subsidy recipients may not be denied rental accommodations because of that income source
rules.requirement: Massachusetts prohibits discrimination in furnishing rental accommodations against a person because they receive federal, state, or local public assistance or housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements. Massachusetts bars employers from requesting criminal offender record information on an initial written job application, except where federal or state law creates mandatory or presumptive disqualification based on convictions or otherwise bars employing people with specified convictions. Massachusetts restricts employment screening by barring employers from requesting or using information about arrests not resulting in conviction, certain older or minor misdemeanor convictions, and sealed or expunged criminal records.
rules.quoted_span: 10. For any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against any individual who is a recipient of federal, state, or local public assistance, including medical assistance, or who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements, because the individual is such a recipient, or because of any requirement of such public assistance, rental assistance, or housing subsidy program.

rules.title: State law allows local rent control and bars unconscionable rent increases as a basis for eviction
rules.requirement: New Jersey has no statewide statute setting rent levels in these documents, but municipalities may adopt rent control or rent leveling ordinances. A landlord seeking eviction for nonpayment of an increased rent must first serve notice, and the increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with municipal rent-control ordinances.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies when a landlord seeks eviction based on a tenant's failure to pay an increased rent.

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act just-cause eviction rules
rules.requirement: New Jersey generally allows eviction from covered residential rental property only for specified good-cause grounds, with ground-specific notice requirements and some relocation protections. The Act also limits nonrenewal without good cause and sets special rules for rent increases, owner occupancy, retirement from residential use, health and safety removals, and condominium/cooperative conversions.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most residential rental properties, including single-family homes, mobile homes and land in a mobile home park, apartment buildings and complexes, and rooming and boarding homes.
rules.exemptions: May not apply to owner-occupied premises with two or three units and two or fewer rental units.; Does not apply to hotel guests, motel guests, or guest houses rented to transient guests or seasonal tenants, except some continual hotel/motel occupants.; Does not apply to a unit held in trust on behalf of an immediate family member who is developmentally disabled and permanently occupies the unit.
rules.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law maximum deposit cap
rules.requirement: For most residential rental properties, a landlord may not collect a security deposit greater than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any annual increase in the security deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. The law does not apply automatically to owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings, though such a tenant may opt in by written request.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most residential rental properties, including mobile homes.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied dwelling.; Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling.
rules.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ). It can be less. Any additional 
yearly security deposit increase may not exceed 10% of the current security deposit.

rules.title: Residential rental property application fee cap
rules.requirement: New Jersey caps residential rental property application or similar fees at $50, with annual CPI-based adjustments beginning January 1 of the year after enactment. The cap does not apply to one-family or two-family dwelling units offered for rent, or to a New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensee unless the licensee is the landlord.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to applications to lease or sublease residential rental property for dwelling purposes.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to a dwelling unit in a one-family or two-family dwelling offered for rent.; Does not apply to a New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensee unless the licensee is the landlord.

rules.requirement: Housing providers generally may not ask about or consider an applicant’s criminal record until after making a conditional offer, and even then may consider only specified convictions within stated lookback periods. rules.title: New Jersey Law Against Discrimination income-source protections
rules.requirement: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination prohibits housing discrimination based on source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment, including refusing to rent solely because a tenant uses a Section 8 voucher. This is an income-source screening restriction enacted by New Jersey, but the provided document is an agency brochure rather than the statutory text.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies broadly to sale or rental of property, including residential rentals, subject to stated exceptions.
rules.exemptions: Exception for rental of a single apartment or flat in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling.; Exception for a single apartment or flat in a two-family dwelling occupied by the owner in the other unit.; Exception for rental of room or rooms in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling.; Exception for room rentals in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling.; Exception for preference given to persons of the same religion by a religious organization in sale, lease, or rental of real property.; Familial-status prohibition does not apply to housing for older persons.

on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent
or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses. This
means, for example, that a landlord cannot deny the
lawful recipient of a Section 8 HUD voucher the right to
rent an apartment based solely on that source of lawful
income.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement: New Jersey prohibits rental property owners, coordinators, and other persons from using or providing algorithmic rent-setting services that perform a coordinating function or facilitate parallel pricing coordination for residential dwelling units. The act defines covered algorithmic devices and coordinating functions, makes violations unlawful under the New Jersey Antitrust Act, bars conflicting municipal ordinances, and directs the Attorney General to receive complaints.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to houses, apartments, accessory units, or other units intended to be used as a primary residence in New Jersey.; Applies to rental property owners that own, directly or indirectly, one or more rental residential dwelling units.
rules.exemptions: Does not cover inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, or detention or correctional facilities.; Does not include certain spreadsheets without AI that require human analysis, or databases that only query unprocessed stored data.; Certain research, public rent estimates, equal-access listing databases, and government affordability controls are excluded from the definition of coordinating function.

rules.title: Newark Rent Control annual rent increase cap
rules.requirement: For covered housing spaces in Newark, annual rent increases at lease expiration or for periodic tenancies are capped at the CPI increase measured from 15 months before the proposed increase month to 3 months before it, with an absolute maximum of 4%. The cap applies no more than once in any consecutive 12-month period regardless of vacancy, tenant turnover, or ownership change, and no increase is allowed unless the dwelling is in substantial compliance and the landlord has met registration requirements.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to housing spaces in multiple dwellings subject to Newark rent control.; Applies when a landlord seeks an increase at lease expiration or for a periodic tenant.
rules.exemptions: Public housing is exempt.; Hotel or motel space rented day-to-day to transients is exempt.; Commercially rented space is exempt.; Newly constructed multiple dwellings and vacant dwellings described in Chapter 19:2 are exempt.; Certain federally or state rehabilitated units receiving Section 8 subsidies or federal vouchers are exempt during the subsidy/program tenure.; Units under a governmental rent-regulation contract are exempt while that governmental agency's authority supersedes Newark's authority.
rules.interaction: supersedes NJ-RENT-01 where it covers the unit
rules.quoted_span: At the expiration of a lease or at the termination of the lease of a periodic tenant, no landlord may request or receive an increase greater than the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the CPI 15 months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase to the CPI three months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase. In no case shall the allowable rent increase exceed 4%.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2017-09-05 (prior enactment/version date, S006)
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents
rules.penalty: The landlord shall rebate to the tenant any amount of rent collected in excess of that permissible pursuant to the terms of this chapter by crediting the tenant with the amount of excess rent paid over a period not to exceed 14 months, or in the event the tenant is no longer in occupancy, by refunding within a one month period. The rebate to the tenant shall be retroactive to two years from the date of the petition.

rules.title: Ban the Box housing screening restrictions
rules.requirement: Landlords and real estate brokers may inquire into and consider an applicant's criminal history only after the applicant has submitted a formal application, must give specified written notice before any criminal history inquiry, and may not consider arrests not resulting in pending charges or conviction, expunged/nullified records, or sealed juvenile records. Newark also limits the lookback periods for most convictions, requires consideration of rehabilitation and related factors, bars ads referencing criminal history, and creates narrow exemptions where other laws require or permit such screening or where housing is designated for people with criminal histories.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rentals, leases, and subleases of real property in Newark.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to rental of a single apartment or flat in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling.; Does not apply to rental of room or rooms in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling.; Exempt where federal or state law, regulation, or rule requires or permits criminal-history consideration, limited to those offenses and time periods.; Exempt for property designated to participate in a government program designed to encourage housing for individuals with criminal histories.
rules.interaction: Where any federal or state law, regulation, or rule requires or permits the consideration of an applicant's criminal history in the rental, lease, or sublease of real property, provided the exemption is limited to those offenses or types of offenses and time periods that federal or state law, regulation, or rule requires or permits the landlord or real estate broker to consider.
rules.quoted_span: Inquiry into and consideration of any applicant's criminal history shall take place only after the applicant has submitted a formal application.
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents
rules.penalty: A first violation shall be subject to a fine of up to $500. Each subsequent violation shall be subject to a fine of up to $1,000.

rules.title: Residential Tenant Protections just-cause eviction and relocation assistance
rules.requirement: San Diego requires just cause to terminate a tenancy in covered residential rental property, defines at-fault and no-fault just causes, requires specified notices to tenants and the Housing Commission, and requires relocation assistance for no-fault terminations. Covered tenants may also have a right of first offer to re-rent within five years after certain no-fault evictions, and noncompliance can void the termination notice.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental property and tenancies lasting more than 30 days.; Applies to a tenancy, meaning the lawful right to occupy for more than 30 days.
rules.exemptions: Transient and tourist hotel occupancy is exempt.; Short-term residential occupancy is exempt.; Deed-restricted affordable housing is exempt.; Housing subject to an affordable-housing subsidy agreement is exempt, except Section 8.; Mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law are exempt.; Specified institutional and nonprofit transitional housing is exempt.; Dormitories owned and operated by educational institutions are exempt.; Property where tenant shares bathroom or kitchen with landlord who lives there is exempt.; Owner-occupied single-family residence with limited rented bedrooms/ADUs/JADUs or a mobilehome is exempt.; A two-unit single structure where landlord occupies one unit as principal residence at the beginning of tenancy and continues in occupancy is exempt.; Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years is exempt unless it is a mobilehome.; Separately alienable residential rental property is exempt if the landlord is not a REIT, corporation, certain LLC, or mobilehome park management and the tenant receives the required written notice of exemption.; For the separately alienable property exemption, the landlord must not be a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management.; For the separately alienable property exemption, tenants must receive the required written exemption notice.
rules.interaction: supersedes CA-JC-01 where it covers the unit
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause. For purposes of this 
Division, just cause includes at-fault just cause and no-fault just cause.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2024-03-28 (amendment, D073)
rules.penalty: A tenant may seek injunctive relief, equitable relief, and money damages, including punitive damages; wrongful eviction damages are not less than three times actual economic damages; failure to provide required relocation assistance makes the landlord liable for not less than three times the required relocation assistance and actual economic damages; the City may enforce with civil and criminal remedies.

rules.title: Source-of-income discrimination and income-standard restrictions
rules.requirement: San Diego prohibits refusing to rent, renew, or continue a tenancy, advertising discrimination, or imposing tenancy terms based on a person's source of income, and it bars financial or income standards that fail to count the tenant's full lawful income or qualifying assistance. Owner-occupied shared kitchen/bathroom arrangements are exempt.
rules.exemptions: Owner or family member resides in the same residential building as the tenant; Owner or family member shares a bathroom or kitchen facility with the tenant or prospective tenant
rules.interaction:
Nothing in this Division shall be deemed to permit a transaction in real property
               that is otherwise prohibited by any applicable law.
rules.quoted_span:
It is unlawful for any person to use a financial or income standard for
                           entering into or renewing a tenancy that does either of the following:

                           (1)    Fails to account for any tenant’s or prospective tenant’s entire
                                  source of income; or

                           (2)    Fails to account for the aggregate source of income of tenants
                                  residing together or proposing to reside together, or the aggregate
                                  source of income of tenants or prospective tenants and their
                                  cosigners or proposed cosigners, on the same basis as the
                                  aggregate source of income of married persons residing together or
                                  proposing to reside together.
rules.conflict_note: Other published dates: 2019-08-01 (private action availability for alleged violations on or after this date, S011)
rules.penalty: Aggrieved person may seek an injunction; court may award monetary damages, including three times one month's rent for violations during or before tenancy, plus punitive damages, attorneys’ fees, and costs.

rules.title: San Diego ban on anti-competitive automated rent price-fixing
rules.requirement: San Diego prohibits selling, licensing, or otherwise providing an algorithmic device to a landlord, and prohibits landlords from using an algorithmic device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property. Covered algorithmic devices use or incorporate algorithms to perform calculations of nonpublic competitor data of two or more landlords to advise or recommend rental rates or occupancy levels; specified reporting, affordable-housing, and appraisal tools are excluded.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental property in the City of San Diego.; Covered software must use or incorporate algorithms to perform calculations of nonpublic competitor data of two or more landlords to advise or recommend rental rates or occupancy levels.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance annual allowable rent increase for rent-controlled units
rules.requirement: For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable increase is 1.6% for the period March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027. The documents also show prior annual allowable increases of 1.4% for March 1, 2025 through February 28, 2026 and 1.7% for March 1, 2024 through February 28, 2025.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rent-controlled units.
rules.exemptions: Newly constructed rental units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979 are exempt from the Ordinance's rent increase limitations.; Tenancies eligible for a rent increase under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act are exempt from the Ordinance's rent increase limitations.; Some tenancies where the rent is regulated by another government agency are exempt from the Ordinance's rent increase limitations.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just-cause eviction requirements
rules.requirement: A landlord may evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance only for one of the 17 just-cause reasons listed in Ordinance Section 37.9(a); expiration of a rental agreement or change in ownership is not just cause. Some tenancies exempt from rent-increase limits are still subject to these eviction protections, including certain post-1979 units and some Costa-Hawkins or agency-regulated tenancies. For tenants evicted under the Ellis Act, the Rent Board publishes relocation payment amounts keyed to the date of service of the eviction notice. For notices served from March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027, the amount is $11,110.05 per tenant, capped at $33,330.13 per unit, plus $7,443.90 for each elderly or disabled tenant.
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental unit is covered by the Rent Ordinance.; Includes tenancies in newly constructed rental units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979.; Includes tenancies eligible for a rent increase under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act.; Includes some tenancies where the rent is regulated by another government agency.
rules.interaction: supersedes CA-JC-01 where it covers the unit
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction. Note that the mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership does not constitute "just cause" for eviction.
rules.effective_date_note: effective date not stated in the documents
rules.penalty: If a landlord evicts or tries to evict a tenant unlawfully, the landlord may be subject to substantial civil and/or criminal liability.

rules.title: San Francisco ban on algorithmic devices used to set rents or manage occupancy
rules.requirement: San Francisco added Section 37.10C to its Rent Ordinance to prohibit the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco. The law defines an algorithmic device as software that uses algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend rents for vacant units, and it allows tenant or City Attorney civil enforcement.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential units in San Francisco.
rules.quoted_span: The law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco.
rules.penalty: A tenant or the City Attorney may bring a civil action for violations.

rules.title: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization Ordinance rent increase cap
rules.requirement: Residential rent increases are limited to the lower of 3% per year or 80% of the percent change in CPI over the most recent 12-month period; if CPI is negative, no rent increase is permitted. The city publishes the annual allowable increase, and the cap does not apply to certain newer buildings and certain mobile home spaces.
rules.exemptions: Residential buildings constructed after February 1, 1995 are exempt from the rent cap.; Mobile home spaces offered for rent after January 1, 1990 are exempt from the rent cap.

rules.title: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.requirement: Santa Ana adopted a just-cause eviction ordinance requiring just cause for termination after 30 days, written notice stating the cause, cure notice before termination for violations, and relocation assistance or rent waiver for certain no-fault terminations. The documents only provide a summary, not the full ordinance text or code citation.
rules.exemptions: Housing produced in the last 15 years is excluded.; Deed-restricted affordable housing is excluded.; Hotels, transient occupancy, hospital and care facilities, dormitories, and other shared living quarters are excluded.

rules.title: Santa Ana bans sale, licensing, and landlord use of algorithmic rent-setting devices using nonpublic competitor data
rules.requirement: Santa Ana Municipal Code Article XXIV prohibits any person from selling, licensing, or otherwise providing an algorithmic device to a landlord, and prohibits landlords from using such a device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property in the city. A tenant may sue for injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; each month of prohibited landlord use and each residential rental property involved is a separate violation.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental property in Santa Ana, including dwellings or units in mobile home parks.
rules.exemptions: Excluded from the definition of algorithmic device are reporting products based on aggregated historical nonpublic competitor data more than 90 days old or public information that do not recommend future rents or occupancy levels.; Excluded from the definition of algorithmic device are products used to establish rental rates or income limits under affordable housing program guidelines.
rules.interaction:
Section 8-3703 — Remedies
(a) A Tenant may seek injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000
per violation of this Article, in a civil action against a Landlord. In an action
brought under this Article, a prevailing Tenant shall recover costs and
reasonable attorney's fees. A prevailing Tenant includes a Tenant granted an
order for injunctive relief. A Lease provision that limits a Tenant from recovering
attorney's fees shall not be enforceable against a Tenant's claim for attorney's

other remedies in this Article or at law, statute, or ordinance.
